newsitem.title: USA: Overseas firms replacing expatriates with local talent.
newsitem.headline: Overseas firms replacing expatriates with local talent.

text.p: U.S.-based multinational firms are replacing significant numbers of their American managers overseas with local hires.
The actions are being taken both to slash the soaring costs of maintaining executives abroad and because local workers frequently respond better to a manager of their own nationality.

"Since 1990, about 25 percent of American expatriates have been replaced by foreign management," said Edward Orchant, president of A-L Associates Inc., a New York-based executive search firm that specialises in placing corporate financial personnel overseas.

"Even though there is an increase in numbers of (American) expatriates abroad because of the increasing number of players (companies operating overseas), over time, fewer Americans will be working abroad," Orchant predicted.
"As soon as the newer companies have their operations set up and running, the cutback process will begin for them," he said.

According to Jim Case, assistant vice president for employer relations at Thunderbird, The American Graduate School of International Management in Glendale, Ariz., "The large, established multinationals that are sophisticated in doing business in multiple markets are at a point in their maturity where they have developed local talent where they don't necessarily have to rely on North Americans as the key managers."

"What has happened is the number of U.S. outbound expatriates in major corporations have probably decreased over the last several years," said Nancy Carter, director of international human resources consulting with KPMG Pete Marwick in New York.

"That does not mean the company is not utilizing its global talent by moving people from country to country. You have a different mix in the global expatriate population. It's not parent-country expatriates only. If anything, the total number of people moving around the world has grown."
Most top corporate managers, Orchant said, "look at this from a cost perspective: it costs too much so bring them home." He called the cost of posting an American overseas "astronomical."

"A two-bedroom apartment in Hong Kong is running $10,000 to $15,000 a month, and sending a kid to an elementary school abroad is anywhere from $5,000 to $15,000 a year. Plus there is the cost of moving families over there and cost-of-living adjustments to executive salaries," Orchant said.
Since 1987, "salary levels increased, peaking in 1991-92" but since then "the trend has been downward," he said.

"The new generation of people just going overseas are definitely not going over with the same benefits package. Overall perks and compensation benefits have been cut in the range of 20 percent or more, depending on the locality," Orchant said.
U.S. candidates for overseas jobs are being told that if they don't want the job, the company can easily find someone local to do it, he said.
"You can go to Singapore and find Singaporeans who were educated at Harvard. That's the best of both worlds for an international company."

One expatriate who will not be recalled even as foreign nationals win promotions, Orchant said, is the senior "shadow." He is the American executive who may hold the title of corporate vice president but who is really responsible for the profitability of the operation. The "shadow" holds the real power, Orchant said.

Otherwise, the expatriate cutback is opening the doors for foreign nationals to rise higher in U.S. companies. "We can expect to see more Asian and Latin faces in the upper levels of American corporations in the future," Orchant said.

Orchant said bilingual and bi-cultural foreign students will be recruited from U.S. business schools such as Thunderbird and given their start in the home office in the United States before going back to their native countries to work for the company there.
(EDITORS: Sherwood Ross is a free-lance writer who covers workplace issues for Reuters. Any opinions in the column are solely those of Mr. Ross.)
